h.en: Introduction, Features and Applications of Java

body.en:
Java is an object-oriented, platform-independent programming language. It was created by James Gosling and his team (called the "Green Team") at Sun Microsystems in 1995; the language was first named Oak and later renamed Java. Oracle Corporation now owns it.

Features of Java (bases of the language)

  • Simple - syntax is like C/C++, so it is easy to learn; there are no pointers, goto or operator overloading.
  • Object oriented - everything is organised inside classes and objects.
  • Platform independent - Write Once, Run Anywhere: compile once into byte code and run the same .class file on Windows, Linux or Mac.
  • Compiled and interpreted - javac compiles to byte code, the JVM interprets it line by line.
  • Robust - strong type checking, exception handling and automatic garbage collection catch errors early.
  • Secure - programs run inside the JVM sandbox; byte code is verified before execution.
  • Multithreaded - several parts of a program can run at the same time.
  • Portable and high performance - the same primitive sizes on every machine; the JIT compiler speeds up hot code.

Applications of Java

  • Android apps - Java was the original language of Android development.
  • Web and enterprise applications - banking systems, e-commerce servers (Spring, JSP).
  • Desktop applications - IDEs like Eclipse and NetBeans are themselves written in Java.
  • Big data and AI - Hadoop, Elasticsearch and libraries like Deeplearning4j run on the JVM.

title.en: 1.2 Writing and Running the First Program

h.en: JDK, JRE, JVM and Byte Code

body.en:
Three names you must distinguish for every exam:

  • JDK (Java Development Kit) - the complete kit for writing programs: the compiler javac, the launcher java, a debugger and other tools. It contains the JRE.
  • JRE (Java Runtime Environment) - everything needed to run a program: class libraries (String, Scanner...) plus the JVM. Ordinary users install only the JRE.
  • JVM (Java Virtual Machine) - the "virtual computer" that executes byte code instruction by instruction (interpreter), with a JIT compiler for speed. It is different for every operating system.

Byte code is the intermediate code stored in .class files after compilation. It is not machine code of any real processor - that is exactly why it is portable.

The life of a Java program has two steps:

  1. Compile: javac Main.java reads the source code and writes Main.class, which contains byte code.
  2. Run: java Main starts the JVM, which loads and verifies the byte code and executes it.
  • C/C++ compile straight to the machine code of one OS, so the result works only on that OS.
  • Java compiles to byte code instead; each OS has its own JVM to execute the same .class file. This is the meaning of Write Once, Run Anywhere.
  • Debug and execute steps are identical on any machine once the JDK is installed.

h.en: Structure of a Java Program and Hello World

body.en:
Every Java program lives inside a class:

  • The file name must match the class name (Main.java for class Main).
  • Execution starts at public static void main(String[] args) - public so that the JVM can call it, static so no object is needed first, void because it returns nothing.
  • Statements end with ;, blocks are wrapped in { }.
  • System.out.println(...) prints a line; System.out is the console, println the method.
  • Java is case sensitive: Main, main and MAIN are three different names.

Run the Hello World program below and study how the output matches each println/print statement.

• A variable is a named memory location that stores a changeable value; a data type fixes what kind of value it can hold and how much memory it uses.
  • Java's 8 primitive types: whole numbers - byte, short, int, long; decimals - float, double; character - char; truth - boolean.
  • Declaring and initializing: int marks = 452; - type, name, initial value, all in one statement. A variable must be initialized (or assigned) before use; Java refuses to read uninitialized local variables.
  • Note the suffixes: L for long values, f for float values.
  • String is a class, not a primitive type - but it is so common that it is written without new: String city = "Surat";.

• Scope tells in which region of code a variable may be used; lifetime tells how long it keeps its memory.
  • A variable declared inside a block { } is a local variable: it is born when the block is entered and dies when the block ends.
  • Inner blocks may use outer variables; outer code may never use a variable declared inside a block.
  • Fields (member variables) of a class live as long as the object lives - scope and lifetime become important again in Unit 2.

• Automatic (widening) conversion: Java itself converts a smaller type into a larger one when no data can be lost: byte -> short -> int -> long -> float -> double. Example: long l = 452;.
  • Manual (narrowing) casting: converting a larger type into a smaller one needs an explicit cast and may lose data: int r = (int) 9.7; gives 9.
  • char and int convert freely using the character's code value ('A' is 65): int code = 'A'; and char nx = (char)('A' + 1); gives 'B'.
  • In mixed expressions Java widens the smaller operand first, so (double) a / b divides exactly while a / b (two ints) drops the fraction.

• Arithmetic: + - * / %; % gives the remainder, integer division discards the fraction.
  • Relational: < > <= >= == != - answers are boolean.
  • Logical: && || ! combine conditions.
  • Assignment: = and shortcuts += -= *= /= %=.
  • Conditional (ternary): condition ? a : b - a one-line if-else that returns a value.
  • Increment/decrement: ++ and --; prefix (++i) changes first, postfix (i++) uses the old value first.
  • Bitwise: & | ^ << >> operate on bits; shifts multiply/divide by powers of 2.

Careful with ==: it compares values for primitives, but objects (like String) are compared with equals().

h.en: Selection: if, if-else, Ladder and Nested if

body.en:
• if runs a block only when its condition is true; if-else gives a second path for false.
  • The if-else-if ladder checks a list of conditions top-down and executes the first true one, then skips the rest - used for ranges like grades.
  • A nested if (an if inside another if) is used when the second question matters only after the first answer, e.g. the maximum-of-three program.

• switch chooses one of many case blocks by matching a single value - cleaner than a long ladder when testing equality.
  • Each case must end with break; otherwise execution falls through into the next case.
  • default catches all unmatched values.
  • Allowed values: char, byte, short, int, and since Java 7 also String.

• for(initialisation; condition; update) - all loop control on one line; the right choice when the count is known (tables, array indexes).
  • while - condition checked before every round; the body may never run. Perfect for "until it becomes zero" algorithms like digit counting.
  • do-while - condition checked after the body, so the body always runs at least once; used for menu-driven programs.
  • The for-each form for (int m : marks) visits every element of an array without an index.

• break leaves the innermost loop or switch immediately - used when the answer is already found and more rounds would be wasted.
  • continue skips only the rest of the current round and starts the next one - used to filter (e.g. skip even numbers).
  • Both are called jump statements; overusing them makes code harder to follow, so use them for clear cases only.

• An array is a single name for a numbered group of same-type values, stored one after another in memory.
  • Declaration: int[] marks;; create: marks = new int[5];; or both with values: int[] marks = {78, 85, 66, 90, 71};.
  • Indexes are 0-based: the first element is marks[0], the last marks[marks.length - 1].
  • marks.length (a field, no brackets) keeps the size - loops that use it survive array resizing automatically.
  • Traverse with an indexed for loop or with for-each; classic tasks are sum/average and min/max in one pass.

• A 2D array is an array of arrays - picture it as a table with rows and columns (a matrix).
  • Declaration with values: int[][] a = {{1,2,3},{4,5,6}}; (2 rows, 3 columns).
  • a.length = number of rows; a[i].length = number of columns in row i.
  • Two nested loops visit every cell; a[i][j] is the element at row i, column j.
  • Matrix addition: add elements at matching positions and store the result in a third matrix of the same shape.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
Hello, World!
Welcome to GTU
Java is simple.

expl.en:
Practical 1(a). Steps: save the file as Main.java, compile with javac Main.java (creates Main.class - byte code), run with java Main (JVM reads the class file).

  • The output window shows the two commands and the printed lines.
  • println moves to a new line after printing; print stays on the same line.
  • // starts a comment, which the compiler ignores.

title.en: Declaring and initializing variables of all primitive types

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
roll = 7
sem = 4
marks = 452
mobile = 9876543210
per = 78.5
cgpa = 8.25
section = A
passed = true

expl.en:
Java has 8 primitive data types. Four store whole numbers (byte, short, int, long), two store decimals (float, double), one stores a single character (char) and one a truth value (boolean).

  • long values end with L and float values with f, otherwise the compiler treats them as int and double.
  • + with a string joins (concatenates) the value to the text.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
add = 22
sub = 12
mul = 85
div = 3
rem = 2
exact = 3.4
cast = 9
code = 65
next = B

expl.en:
Practical 1(b). Integer division throws the decimal part away: 17/5 gives 3. To get the exact answer, cast one operand to double before dividing.

  • Widening (automatic, no data loss): byte -> short -> int -> long -> float -> double; char -> int.
  • Narrowing (manual cast, possible data loss): (int) 9.7 cuts the fraction and keeps 9.
  • The remainder operator % returns what is left after division (17 % 5 = 2).

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
x = 10
y = 20
x + y = 30
x again = 10

expl.en:
Scope = where a variable can be used; lifetime = how long it exists.

  • A variable is usable only inside the block { } where it is declared. When the block ends, the variable dies.
  • Inner blocks can see outer variables (z = x + y works), but outer code cannot see variables declared inside (y = 30; after the block would be a compile error - it is commented out here, try removing the // to see the error yourself in a lab).
  • Because dead variables disappear quickly, Java programs stay memory-efficient.

title.en: Operators: arithmetic, relational, logical, bitwise, ternary, ++/--

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
a/b = 3
a%b = 1
a>b = true
both = true
a&b = 2
a|b = 11
a^b = 9
a<<1 = 20
max = 10
c = 10
d = 12

expl.en:
• Arithmetic: + - * / %. Wrap arithmetic in brackets inside println - "a/b = " + a / b would not even compile, because + joins the string to a first and then tries to divide a string.
  • Relational: > < >= <= == != give true/false. Logical: && || !
  • Bitwise: 10 = 1010 and 3 = 0011 in binary, so a&b=2 (0010), a|b=11 (1011), a^b=9 (1001); a << 1 shifts bits left = 20.
  • Ternary: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse.
  • a++ uses the old value then increments (c = 10, afterwards a = 11); ++a increments first (d = 12).

title.en: if, if-else and if-else-if ladder (result grades)

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
Result: Pass
Type: First
Grade: A

expl.en:
• Simple if runs its statement only when the condition is true.
  • if-else chooses between two paths.
  • Ladder checks conditions from top and runs the FIRST true branch - so put the highest limit first (70 before 35); otherwise 72 would wrongly fall into a lower grade.
  • For a single statement the braces { } are optional.

title.en: Nested if-else: maximum of three numbers

expl.en:
Practical 2(a). An if inside another if is a nested if. The program first compares a with b, then compares the winner with c and stores the greatest number in g.

  • Indentation (inner code shifted right) makes nested logic readable.
  • Short alternative: Math.max(a, Math.max(b, c)), or one ternary expression.

title.en: switch-case: day of the week and a simple menu

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
Wednesday
result = 12

expl.en:
• switch compares one value against many case labels; the matching block runs.
  • break is compulsory: without it, execution falls through into the next case (a famous interview question).
  • default runs when no case matches.
  • Since Java 7, switch works on String too, as the small calculator menu shows.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
Table of 7:
1 x 7 = 7
2 x 7 = 14
3 x 7 = 21
4 x 7 = 28
5 x 7 = 35
digits = 3
k = 5
k = 4
k = 3
k = 2
k = 1

expl.en:
• for(init; condition; step) - best when the number of repetitions is known.
  • while tests the condition first; if it is false at the start, the body never runs.
  • do-while tests after the body, so the body always runs at least once (useful for menus).
  • The digit-counting trick divides by 10 repeatedly - a very common exam question.

title.en: Sum of digits of a number (while loop)

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
number = 4782
sum = 21

expl.en:
Practical 2(b). The classic digit-splitting pattern:

  • n % 10 peels off the last digit, n / 10 removes it.
  • Repeat until the number becomes 0; add each digit into sum.
  • Dry run for 4782: 2 + 8 + 7 + 4 = 21.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
odd numbers 1..9: 1 3 5 7 9 
big = 12

expl.en:
• continue skips only the current iteration; the loop keeps going.
  • break ends the loop at once - e.g. after finding what we were searching for.
  • The for-each loop for (int s : stops) walks through every element of an array without an index.

title.en: 1D array: declaration, traversal, sum and average

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
All marks:
0 : 78
1 : 85
2 : 66
3 : 90
4 : 71
sum = 390
average = 78.0

expl.en:
Practical 3(a).

  • An array stores many values of one type under one name; indexes run from 0 to length-1.
  • marks.length gives the number of elements (no brackets - it is a field, not a method).
  • 1.0 * sum makes the division decimal, so the average keeps its fraction.

Practical 3(b).

  • A 2D array is an array of arrays - here a 2x3 matrix.
  • a.length is the number of rows and a[0].length the number of columns.
  • Nested loops visit every cell; corresponding cells are added into sum[i][j].
  • The inner print stays on the same line; after each row println() jumps to the next line, forming the matrix layout. Genuine output: 8 10 12 / 5 7 9.

title.en: Finding smallest and largest in an array

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
smallest = 9
largest = 55

expl.en:
The scan-and-remember pattern:

  • Assume the first element is the answer, then compare it with every element; whenever a smaller/larger value appears, remember it.
  • Runs in one pass - a favourite GTU 4-marker.

• The outer loop fixes the row number; the inner loop prints that row's characters.
  • Row i of pattern 1 prints i stars; the inner loop's limit depends on i - this dependency is the key idea of every pattern program.
  • Pattern 2 counts down (4 to 1) and prints the numbers descending in each row.

q.en: Who developed Java and in which year?

a.en: James Gosling with the Green Team at Sun Microsystems, in 1995; the language was first called Oak.

q.en: What is Java?

a.en: An object-oriented, platform-independent programming language that is both compiled (to byte code) and interpreted (by the JVM).

q.en: Give five features of Java.

a.en: Simple, object oriented, platform independent, robust, secure; also multithreaded, portable and high performance.

q.en: Why is Java called platform independent?

a.en: javac produces byte code, not machine code; the same .class file runs on any OS because every OS has its own JVM.

q.en: Name four application areas of Java.

a.en: Android apps, web and enterprise servers, desktop applications, and big data / AI tools.

q.en: What are JDK, JRE and JVM?

a.en: JDK = development kit for writing programs (javac + tools), contains JRE; JRE = runtime environment (libraries + JVM); JVM = virtual machine that executes byte code.

q.en: What is byte code?

a.en: The intermediate, OS-independent code that javac writes into .class files; the JVM executes it.

q.en: Write the commands to compile and run Main.java.

a.en: javac Main.java (compile to Main.class) and java Main (run on the JVM).

q.en: What does 'Write Once, Run Anywhere' mean?

a.en: Compile the program a single time into byte code and run the same file on every operating system.

q.en: Which method starts every Java program?

a.en: public static void main(String[] args).

q.en: Why must main() be public and static?

a.en: public so the JVM can call it from outside; static so it can run without creating an object first.

q.en: What does void in main() mean?

a.en: The method returns nothing.

q.en: Why must the file be saved as Main.java?

a.en: The file name must match the class name declared inside it.

q.en: Is Java case sensitive?

a.en: Yes: Main, main and MAIN are different names.

q.en: Difference between print() and println()?

a.en: println adds a new line after printing; print stays on the same line.

q.en: List the 8 primitive data types of Java.

a.en: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean.

q.en: What are the sizes of int and double?

a.en: int = 4 bytes, double = 8 bytes.

q.en: Why do we write 9876543210L and 78.5f?

a.en: Without L the number is treated as int (too large here); without f a decimal is treated as double and cannot go into a float.

q.en: Is String a primitive type?

a.en: No, String is a class; but Java allows the easy literal form String s = "Hi";.

q.en: What is a variable?

a.en: A named memory location whose value can change; in Java it must be declared with a type before use.

q.en: Define scope and lifetime of a variable.

a.en: Scope = the region of code where the variable can be used (its block); lifetime = how long it exists (block entry to block end).

q.en: Can outer code use a variable declared inside { }?

a.en: No - the variable dies when the block ends; using it outside is a compile error.

q.en: What is the difference between widening and narrowing?

a.en: Widening converts a smaller type to a larger one automatically without data loss; narrowing needs a manual cast and may lose data.

q.en: What does (int) 9.7 do?

a.en: A narrowing cast: the fraction is cut, so the value is 9.

q.en: What is the output of char ch = 'A' + 1?

a.en: 'A' + 1 is int 66; assigning back to char needs a cast: (char)('A'+1) gives 'B'.

q.en: Why does 17/5 print 3 but (double)17/5 prints 3.4?

a.en: int/int is integer division; casting one operand to double makes it decimal division.

q.en: Name the groups of operators in Java.

a.en: Arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, conditional (ternary), increment/decrement, bitwise.

q.en: Difference between i++ and ++i?

a.en: i++ uses the old value then increments; ++i increments first and uses the new value.

q.en: What does the ternary operator do?

a.en: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse - a one-line if-else that returns a value.

q.en: What is the operator precedence problem in "sum = " + a + b?

a.en: It joins as text (sum = 105); to add first, write "sum = " + (a + b).

q.en: Why is 17 % 5 equal to 2?

a.en: % is the remainder operator: 17 = 5 x 3 + 2.

q.en: When do you use an if-else-if ladder?

a.en: When several ranges are tested, like grade calculation; the first true branch runs.

q.en: What is a nested if?

a.en: An if statement placed inside another if (or else) block.

q.en: Why must each case in switch end with break?

a.en: Without break, execution falls through and the following cases also run.

q.en: Can switch work on strings?

a.en: Yes, since Java 7 switch accepts String values.

q.en: Differentiate while and do-while.

a.en: while tests before the body (may run zero times); do-while tests after, so the body always runs at least once.

q.en: When is the for loop preferred?

a.en: When the number of repetitions is known in advance.

q.en: What is the role of break and continue?

a.en: break exits the innermost loop or switch immediately; continue skips to the next iteration.

q.en: What is the difference between length in arrays and length() in String?

a.en: length is a field of an array; length() is a method of the String class.

q.en: How are array elements numbered?

a.en: From 0 to length-1; marks[0] is the first element.

q.en: How do you create an array of 5 integers?

a.en: int[] a = new int[5]; or with values int[] a = {78, 85, 66, 90, 71};.

q.en: What is a 2D array?

a.en: An array of arrays, viewed as rows and columns; a[0].length is the number of columns.

q.en: Why are two loops used for matrix addition?

a.en: The outer loop selects the row i and the inner loop the column j, so every cell m[i][j] is added.

q.en: What is the sum-of-digits algorithm?

a.en: while n != 0: add n % 10 and set n = n / 10, until the number becomes 0.

q.en: What is for-each loop in Java?

a.en: for (int m : marks) - visits each element of the array without an index variable.
